column5: vengeance and recompense reserved for a day
column6: The commentary glosses dīn as recompense and makes the day an arriving event; Moses' song says vengeance and recompense are reserved for the day when the enemy's foot slips, joining both images in one judgment formula.

column5: YHWH comes to judge the earth
column6: The commentary describes the day as an event that arrives and the balance as just measure; the psalm says YHWH comes to judge the world in righteousness, making arrival and equitable judgment one scene.

column5: acquittal and wicked balances
column6: The commentary joins fraudulent weighing to final accounting; Micah asks whether one can acquit someone who uses wicked scales and deceitful weights, making the crooked balance a matter for judgment.

column5: God demands an account for blood
column6: The commentary's branch gloss says blood may be lost if not avenged; Genesis says God will require an accounting for human blood, adding explicit divine reckoning for bloodshed.

column5: blood pollution; only the killer's blood atones
column6: The commentary's root branch describes a death claim converted to blood-price; Numbers says blood pollutes the land and homicide cannot be atoned for except by the blood of the one who shed it, a specific legal contrast to monetary substitution.

column5: righteous people cannot deliver another's life
column6: The commentary says no one can replace another's liability on the day; Ezekiel says even Noah, Daniel and Job would deliver only themselves, not sons or daughters, specifying the limit on a righteous person's rescue of kin.

column5: one bears one's own iniquity
column6: The commentary's final account admits no substitute payment; Ezekiel says the son does not bear the father's guilt and the sinner's own soul dies, making responsibility individual.

column5: the price of life's redemption is beyond reach
column6: The commentary develops price, equivalent and full measure, then says a ransom cannot settle the final account; the psalm says life's redemption is too costly and beyond payment, explaining why no human can buy another free.

column5: God alone redeems from Sheol
column6: After saying no person can ransom a brother, the psalmist says God will redeem his life from Sheol; this qualifies the commentary's no-exchange image by locating rescue with God rather than a human payer.

column5: dominion given to the humanlike figure
column6: The commentary makes the day God's sovereign domain; after the court scene, Daniel gives the humanlike figure everlasting dominion and a kingdom, adding a royal succession scene within judgment.

column5: the court removes the ruler's dominion
column6: The commentary defines the malik branch through authority and command; Daniel's court sits to remove the persecuting ruler's dominion, showing judgment as an actual transfer of power.

column5: coming ruler brings recompense
column6: The commentary's king has a strong hand and the day arrives with repayment; Isaiah says the Lord comes with might, his arm rules, and recompense is with him, meeting sovereignty and repayment in one image.

column5: dead revived; living judged
column6: The commentary links the q-w-m branch to resurrection and people standing before God; Avot says the dead will live again and the living will be judged, an especially compact Jewish formulation of the whole scene.

column5: no forgetfulness, favoritism or bribes
column6: The commentary notes witness-memory failure and says an offered equivalent is rejected; Avot says the Judge has no forgetting, favoritism or acceptance of bribes and that all is according to reckoning, directly sharpening both details.

column5: settle with an accuser before court
column6: The commentary makes a debt due under judgment its central image; Jesus tells a debtor to settle with his accuser on the way to court before the judge hands him over, adding urgency before a judicial account closes.

column5: last coin owed until paid
column6: The commentary links a full-weight coin to the debt's final settlement; Jesus says the prisoner will not leave until paying the last quadrans, making even a small coin part of complete collection.

column5: Son of Man comes and repays each person
column6: The commentary joins the arriving day, sovereign rule and recompense; Jesus says the Son of Man comes in the Father's glory and repays each according to conduct, a direct Christian formulation of that combined scene.

column5: each receives for deeds before Christ's tribunal
column6: The commentary says the day is an individual account with no one absent; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive for what they did in the body, specifying personal recompense.

column5: sea and death surrender their dead
column6: The commentary says people cannot be absent from the day of account; Revelation says the sea, Death and Hades give up their dead for judgment, closing imagined routes of disappearance.

column5: mercy triumphs over judgment
column6: The commentary recalls that a victim's kin may forgive and that payment should be gracious; James says judgment is without mercy to one who showed no mercy, while mercy triumphs over judgment, linking interpersonal mercy to the final account.

column5: Deuteronomy's vengeance applied as warning
column6: The commentary glosses divine anger as punishment and dīn as recompense; Hebrews quotes “vengeance is mine, I will repay” and “the Lord will judge his people” from Deuteronomy to warn its hearers, giving those Hebrew formulas a Christian judgment setting.

column5: leaving the straight way
column6: The commentary contrasts a straight path with those who stray; Peter says false teachers have left the straight way and followed Balaam's path, giving apostasy a concrete route image.

column5: make straight paths for feet
column6: The commentary asks for guidance on a straight path; Hebrews tells its hearers to make straight paths for their feet so the lame may be healed, turning the path image into communal moral practice.

column5: the Son of Man sits on a glorious throne
column6: The commentary calls the day the sovereign's domain; Jesus' judgment scene opens with the Son of Man coming in glory and sitting on his throne, adding the ruler's enthronement before the separation already described nearby.

column5: nations taught to walk in God's paths
column6: The commentary asks for guidance on the straight path; Micah pictures nations going to Zion to be taught God's ways and walk in his paths, adding a public, communal destination to the prayer for guidance.

column5: God judges and arbitrates among nations
column6: The commentary places the path under the sovereign's judgment; Micah says God judges among peoples and arbitrates for many nations, connecting divine rule to just decisions among communities.

column5: the righteous stand before their oppressors
column6: The commentary connects rising to the final division of people; Wisdom says the righteous will stand with confidence before those who afflicted them, adding a reversal in which the formerly oppressed are vindicated.

column5: first judgment question concerns honest business
column6: The commentary develops debt, exchange and dishonest scales as ethical matters; the Talmud says a person is first asked at judgment whether business was conducted faithfully, bringing commercial honesty directly into the afterlife account.

column5: ransom for an ox owner's liability
column6: The commentary says a life claim can be converted to blood-price and later says no ransom works on the judgment day; Exodus permits a ransom for the owner of a lethal ox, a sharply bounded Torah case that clarifies which kind of liability can be exchanged for payment.

column5: unjust rulers are judged for not walking rightly
column6: The commentary defines the malik branch as command over a community and connects the straight path to right conduct; Wisdom rebukes rulers for not ruling rightly or walking according to God's will, tying royal authority to a path by which it is judged.
